Ipso facto: A common English idiom with a similar meaning is "in and of itself". Ipso facto: e.g., "Faustus had signed his life away, and was, ipso facto, incapable of repentance" (fr In contrast, de facto ("in fact" or "in practice") describes situations that are generally known to exist in reality, even if not legally authorized.[2] The terms are often used to contrast different scenarios, for example, "I know that, de jure, this is supposed to be a parking lot, but now that the flood has left four feet of water here, it’s a de facto swimming pool".[3] Ipso facto: Compare also "by itself" and "per se". Musical notation: Other common time signatures are "3/4" (three beats per bar, with each beat being a quarter note); "2/4" (two beats per bar, with each beat being a quarter note); "6/8" (six beats per bar, with each beat being an eighth note) and "12/8" (twelve beats per bar, with each beat being an eighth note; in practice, the eighth notes are typically put into four groups of three eighth notes. Half note: In time signatures with 4 as the bottom number, such as 4/4 or 3/4 time, the half note is two beats long. Half note: In music, a half note (American) or minim (British) is a note played for half the duration of a whole note (or semibreve) and twice the duration of a quarter note (or crotchet). Half note: It was given its Latin name (minim, meaning "least or smallest") because it was the shortest of the five note values used in early medieval music notation .
